reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Hydrocephalus reflects an imbalance between cerebrospinal fluid production and absorption or a blockage to its flow, producing ventricular enlargement
It is broadly divided into obstructive (non-communicating), where flow is blocked within the ventricular system, and communicating, where absorption at the arachnoid granulations is impaired
Acute obstructive hydrocephalus is a neurosurgical emergency presenting with headache, vomiting, reduced consciousness, and papilloedema from rapidly rising intracranial pressure
In infants, before fusion of the sutures, features include an enlarging head circumference, bulging fontanelle, splayed sutures, and the sunsetting sign of downward-deviated eyes
Normal pressure hydrocephalus classically presents in older adults with the triad of gait apraxia, cognitive decline, and urinary incontinence, and gait often improves after CSF drainage
Treatment principles include relieving the obstruction where possible and diverting CSF, commonly by ventriculoperitoneal shunting or endoscopic third ventriculostomy for suitable obstructive cases
Shunt complications such as infection, blockage, over-drainage, and disconnection are common and should be considered in any shunted patient who deteriorates
Imaging helps distinguish true hydrocephalus with raised pressure from ex vacuo ventricular enlargement due to brain atrophy
reference.pathophysiology: Hydrocephalus is an abnormal accumulation of cerebrospinal fluid within the ventricular system, usually resulting in ventricular dilatation and, when acute, raised intracranial pressure. CSF is produced largely by the choroid plexus, circulates through the ventricles and subarachnoid space, and is absorbed at the arachnoid granulations. Obstruction along this pathway (for example at the aqueduct, fourth ventricular outflow, or by a mass or blood clot) causes non-communicating hydrocephalus, while impaired absorption after haemorrhage, infection, or inflammation causes communicating hydrocephalus. Rising pressure and ventricular expansion compress adjacent white matter and, if unrelieved, can lead to herniation.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebral atrophy with ex vacuo ventriculomegaly
Shunt malfunction in a previously treated patient
additionalInvestigations: CT or MRI brain to assess ventricular size, the level of obstruction, and periventricular changes
MRI with CSF flow studies when aqueductal or outflow obstruction is suspected
Head circumference monitoring and cranial ultrasound in infants with an open fontanelle
Large-volume lumbar puncture or external drainage trial to predict shunt response in suspected NPH
Shunt series and imaging to evaluate suspected shunt malfunction
redFlags: Acute obstructive hydrocephalus with falling conscious level, severe headache, and vomiting requiring emergency CSF diversion
Signs of impending herniation from rapidly rising intracranial pressure
Rapidly enlarging head with bulging fontanelle and sunsetting eyes in an infant
Shunt malfunction or shunt infection presenting with headache, drowsiness, or fever in a shunted patient
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause, speed of onset, and timeliness of treatment; well-selected patients do well after CSF diversion, but outcomes are limited by the underlying pathology and by recurrent shunt complications, and untreated acute obstruction can be rapidly fatal.
pitfalls: Mistaking ex vacuo ventriculomegaly from atrophy for treatable hydrocephalus
Delaying CSF diversion in acute obstructive hydrocephalus while awaiting further tests
Overlooking shunt malfunction as a cause of deterioration in a shunted patient
Attributing the NPH triad solely to ageing or dementia and missing a reversible component
management: Cerebrospinal fluid diversion is the definitive treatment, most commonly ventriculoperitoneal shunting, with endoscopic third ventriculostomy for suitable obstructive cases
Treatment of the underlying cause where possible, such as resection of an obstructing tumour or clearance of a clot
Emergency external ventricular drainage for acute obstructive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure
Shunt insertion in normal pressure hydrocephalus for patients selected by a positive large-volume lumbar puncture or external drainage trial
Long-term shunt surveillance with prompt imaging and shunt series for suspected malfunction, and revision or antibiotic treatment for shunt infection
Head circumference monitoring and cranial ultrasound in infants with an open fontanelle
Multidisciplinary neurosurgical follow-up with attention to neurodevelopmental outcome
